name: Woodland Brown
lede: Woodland Brown is a near-black brown that our archive finds in more paintings than any other color, nearly one in six.

sections.title: A near-black brown
sections.body: Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary dates Woodland Brown to 1925, plate 8, chip H8 [1]. The ISCC-NBS revision of 1955 files the same chip as "dark grayish yellow brown," block 81 [1]. Its nearest named neighbor is [[blackish-brown]], barely distinguishable by eye, with [[chocolate-brown]] close behind [2]. Further out, [[reddish-black]] and [[brown-olive]] sit in the same small cluster [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds a match for Woodland Brown in 3,602 of 23,781 paintings, about 15.2 percent, more common than 98 percent of the named colors we track [3]. It peaks in the 1600s, in 816 of 6,394 paintings, though only 1.2 times the rate expected from that century's share of the archive, since it is common throughout [3]. Inside a painting it most often sits as a mid-tone, in 44 percent of its appearances [3]. It is most over-represented in paintings of Tibet, 3.1 times the expected rate, though the sample is small, 12 of 47 [3]. The earliest archive match dates to 1099, eight centuries before Maerz and Paul recorded the name in 1930 [3]. It also shares canvases more than chance with colors we call Plain mouse and Coffee, a pairing common in interiors and still lifes [3]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, read as screen colors, not pigment identifications[3].
